questions.enonce_markdown:
Briefly describe the following processes that take place during the transmission of an impulse:

(i) Resting potential.

(ii) Action potential.

(iii) Threshold of stimulation.

(iv) Repolarization.

(v) Absolute refractory period.

(vi) Saltatory conduction. *[12 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Resting potential.** The **potential difference across the membrane of a neurone that is not conducting an impulse**: the inside is **negative relative to the outside, about -70 mV** (the membrane is said to be **polarised**). It is maintained by (1) the **sodium-potassium pump**, which moves **3 Na$^+$ out for every 2 K$^+$ in** using ATP, and (2) the membrane being **much more permeable to K$^+$** (leak channels) than to Na$^+$, so K$^+$ diffuses out faster than Na$^+$ enters, while large negatively charged organic ions stay inside.

**(ii) Action potential.** A **rapid, temporary reversal of the membrane potential** (inside becomes positive, about +40 mV) when the neurone is stimulated. **Voltage-gated Na$^+$ channels open**, Na$^+$ **rushes in** and the membrane is **depolarised**. It lasts about 1 to 2 ms, obeys the **all-or-nothing law** (the size is the same whatever the strength of the stimulus above threshold) and is the nerve impulse that travels along the axon.

**(iii) Threshold of stimulation.** The **minimum strength of stimulus** (depolarisation to about -50 mV) needed to open enough voltage-gated Na$^+$ channels to **trigger an action potential**. A stimulus below the threshold produces only a local, graded change and **no impulse**; at or above it, a full action potential is produced.

**(iv) Repolarization.** The **return of the membrane potential to its resting value** after depolarisation: the Na$^+$ channels **close (inactivate)** and the **voltage-gated K$^+$ channels open**, so **K$^+$ diffuses out** and the inside becomes negative again (often briefly more negative than at rest, **hyperpolarisation**). The sodium-potassium pump then restores the original distribution of Na$^+$ and K$^+$.

**(v) Absolute refractory period.** The **short time (about 1 to 2 ms) just after an action potential, during which the neurone cannot be stimulated again, however strong the stimulus**, because the **Na$^+$ channels are inactivated** and cannot reopen until the membrane has repolarised. It makes the impulse **travel in one direction only**, keeps impulses **separate (discrete)** and limits the **maximum frequency** of impulses.

**(vi) Saltatory conduction.** In a **myelinated axon**, the **myelin sheath** (made by Schwann cells) is an **electrical insulator**, so ions can cross the membrane only at the **nodes of Ranvier**, where the voltage-gated channels are concentrated. The action potential **jumps from node to node** by local currents between nodes. It is **much faster** (up to about 100 m s$^{-1}$, compared with about 1 m s$^{-1}$ in unmyelinated axons of similar size) and **uses less energy**, since fewer ions have to be pumped back.

questions.enonce_markdown: Using suitable illustrations, describe the mechanism of impulse transmission across the synapse. *[8 marks]* *(12, 8 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **synapse** is the junction between two neurones (separated by a **synaptic cleft about 20 nm wide**). In a **cholinergic synapse** the impulse is carried across by the neurotransmitter **acetylcholine (ACh)**.

**Structure.** The **presynaptic knob** contains many **mitochondria** and **synaptic vesicles filled with acetylcholine**, and its membrane has **voltage-gated Ca$^{2+}$ channels**. The **postsynaptic membrane** has **receptor proteins** for ACh linked to **chemically (ligand) gated Na$^+$ channels**.

**Mechanism**

1. An **action potential arrives** at the presynaptic knob and **depolarises** its membrane.
2. **Voltage-gated Ca$^{2+}$ channels open** and **Ca$^{2+}$ diffuse in** from the cleft.
3. The Ca$^{2+}$ cause the **synaptic vesicles to move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane**, releasing ACh into the cleft by **exocytosis**.
4. ACh **diffuses across the cleft** and **binds to the receptors** on the postsynaptic membrane.
5. The **chemically gated Na$^+$ channels open**, Na$^+$ **enter** the postsynaptic neurone and cause **depolarisation** (an excitatory postsynaptic potential, EPSP). If the **threshold** is reached, a **new action potential** is set up in the postsynaptic neurone and travels along it. Several small EPSPs can add up (summation).
6. The ACh is **quickly broken down by the enzyme acetylcholinesterase** into **choline and ethanoic (acetic) acid**, which stops the stimulation (otherwise the postsynaptic neurone would fire continuously) and clears the receptors. The **Ca$^{2+}$ are pumped out** of the knob.
7. Choline and ethanoate are **taken back into the presynaptic knob**, where **ATP from the mitochondria** is used to **resynthesise ACh**, which is stored in vesicles again.

Because the transmitter is released on one side only and the receptors are on the other, the impulse crosses the synapse **in one direction only**. There is a **synaptic delay of about 0.5 ms**.

**Illustrations expected.** (1) A labelled drawing of the synapse (presynaptic knob with vesicles, mitochondria and Ca$^{2+}$ channels; the cleft; the postsynaptic membrane with receptors and Na$^+$ channels). (2) A sequence of small diagrams (or arrows) showing steps 1 to 7: calcium entry, vesicle fusion, diffusion and binding of ACh, Na$^+$ entry, breakdown by acetylcholinesterase and recycling of the products.
